AFTER ESIDIMENI

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
With the arbitration award announced, we ask the Esidimeni tragedy brought any change? We investigate the current conditions of Esidimeni survivors and other psychiatric patients in Gauteng.

Unique Selling Point:
We unpack the arbitration award and reflect on the families' views of the outcome, while asking whether this experience has done anything to improve mental health care in Gauteng.

After the Esidimeni tragedy, the surviving Gauteng state psychiatric patients were removed from the deadly NGOs and placed in state psychiatric hospitals or private facilities, some even into Life facilities. But are they better off now? There are complaints from family members that patients are still lacking proper care. The family committee says they want to have access to documents like the service level agreements between the provincial health department and the facilities - it is simply no longer good enough to hear that such documents exist. Meanwhile, other patients still remain at some of the NGOs where people died. Insiders tell us of the terrible conditions at two NGOs in Cullinan. Is the Gauteng Health Department just paying lip service when they promise to do betteR?

Summary:
In the aftermath of the Esidimeni tragedy, the survivors of the Gauteng Mental Health Marathon project were moved to psychiatric hospitals and other facilities. In general, their living conditions are much improved from the NGOs where they were starving and freezing. But the family committee raises concerns that they do not have access to service level agreements between the health department and facilities to see whwther they are satisfied with the level of care agreed upon for their loved ones. Some families complain that patients are not getting proper care. Some facilities are not fit for purpose and there is still a lack of linen, toiletries and other things. One family member told us that her sister's ID was still with the owner of the NGO until very recently - the department had not taken steps to collect the IDs and Sassa cards until she queried it. We talk to family members and plan to visit facilities to see for ourselves.

Even though the former Esidimeni patients were moved, some of the NGOs where patients died, remain open and other patients are still living there. Peter Mentoor, who used to work as a security guard at an NGO in Cullinan, says he left because he ccould not stand the way patients were mistreated. He says he was made to sleep in the ward with the patients and there were no qualified care workers at night. He says male and female patients are housed together and patients are not being fed and clothed properly.

Meanwhile, the police and the Gauteng health department are also still looking for some patients who had gone missing during the move. The health department had simply lost track of nearly 50 patients -- for months, no one knew where they were. Some of these patients have since been found still living at some of the "death NGOs" We track what happened to these patients who have been found, and question what could have happened to those still missing.

Press Release:



Life After Esidimeni
The families of the Esidimeni tragedy have been awarded R1.2-million each as compensation for the lives lost in the tragedy. Retired deputy chief justice Dikgang Moseneke made damning observations in his arbitration award about the sheer lack of accountability for the lives of patients, saying senior officials had lied, played victim and violated the constitution. Carte Blanche asks: while responsibility has been apportioned, will it improve the state of mental health care services?




Script:


SCRIPT: AFTER ESIDIMENI
PRODUCERS: Anna-Maria van Niekerk & Marzanne van den Berg
PRESENTER: Devi Sankaree-Govender
TX: 25 March 2018
DURATION: 11 minutes

JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Virginia Machpelah, Matsobane John Mahloko, Christopher Makhoba ...
These are some of the victims of the Esidimeni tragedy to whom Judge Dikgang Moseneke paid tribute last week. His judgment was the culmination of 45 days of hearings in an arbitration process that families and government had agreed on.
JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: This is a harrowing account of the death, torture and disappearance of utterly vulnerable mental health care users in the care of an admittedly delinquent provincial government.
The tragedy ensued after the Gauteng Health Department suddenly decided to move 1711 state patients from private Life Esidimeni facilities, where they had been housed for decades, to ill-equipped, unprepared non-governmental organisations. The department said it could no longer afford Life Esidimeni. At the NGOs, many of the severely mentally ill patients, in the care of the state, were left without medication, food, water and clothing to keep them warm through winter. 144 patients died.
DEVI LINK TO CAMERA: Carte Blanche witnessed every step of the families’ journey to seek answers and accountability. It began when Christine Nxumalo discovered her sister Virginia Machpelah’s inexplicable death at a Pretoria NGO.
STRAP: CARTE BLANCHE AUGUST 2017: Ethel, Ethel, Ethel, I want to see the room where she was in...want to see the condition of the place where she was staying…
Moseneke awarded each family R1.2 million in damages for violated rights, trauma and funeral expenses.
DEVI LINK TO CAMERA: All along, families have had two questions: Why, and who was responsible? The arbitration hearings were supposed to be a way to find truth, closure and redress. But after it all, emotions are mixed.
ANDREW PETERSEN, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: It was never, never about the money.
Andrew Petersen found his uncle Victor Truter emaciated at Mosego Home in Krugersdorp after the move.
ANDREW PETERSEN, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: You know, the money helps, but it was always about sending a strong message to government...that also will create a momentum that will challenge this laidback sort of culture we have in government and civil service.
Nxumalo and other families feel vindicated now that Moseneke joined all the dots.
CHRISTINE NXUMALO, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: When I heard my sister’s name, it was like phew, this is real. It’s not some kind of a dream or some imaginary thing, you know, we experienced it. It was like the constitution suddenly, it was flexing its muscles…I swear it was almost a beautiful moment in such a sad situation.
Over the years, Carte Blanche inspected the notorious NGOs -- they in turn pointed to the Health Department who had neglected to give them time, money and support.
JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: These NGOs turned out to be sites of death and torture.
Moseneke reserved his harshest words for the former top 3 at Gauteng Health: MEC Qedani Mahlangu, head of department Dr Barney Selebano and Mental Health Director Dr Makgabo Manamela. All three have resigned. The full record of the hearings will go to the police for investigation.
JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Miss Mahlangu was responsible. She was the ultimate leader and commander of the project.
The NPA said it’s received 140 dockets from police. It’s now up to them to decide whether anyone must be charged. // Boitumelo Mangena’s mother, Rahab, who suffered from dementia, was moved without their knowledge. Her brother found her at the overcrowded Takalani Home.
BOITUMELO MANGENA, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: He said he found her sitting in the corner in a chair, no blankets, no shoes on, no socks on and she was still in her Life Esidimeni outfit. So in those two weeks that she had not … been changed or anything.
While the siblings were trying to arrange to take her home, she died of a heart attack that they believe was caused by the conditions.
BOITUMELO MANGENA, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: You go into the arbitration process thinking I’m going to find answers. I’m going to find closure, I’m going to find healing. And the end comes and there’s none of that.
Survivors were mostly moved back to private facilities or state psychiatric hospitals.
CHRISTINE NXUMALO, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: And one of the requests that we ask the Department of Health was that there must be an audit at the end of this process. We need to know exactly what happened to everybody.
At provincial headquarters, Col Lungelo Dlamini said police have tracked down only 13 patients who went missing in the move. 1 had passed away.
LUNGELO DLAMINI, GAUTENG SAPS SPOKESMAN: At this stage there are 49 people that are still missing -- the investigation is still continuing in that regard.
The hearings revealed there are about 5000 psychiatric patients at NGOs in Gauteng. At the South African Depression and Anxiety Group, Cassey Chambers is concerned
CASSEY CHAMBERS, OPERATIONS DIRECTOR, SADAG: A lot of these facilities were running before Esidimeni, so there are still patients that are at Takalani, Mosego Home that were kind of left behind and I think the real question is how we’re monitoring and checking up on those patients.
Shammah House in Cullinan, outside Pretoria, had Esidimeni patients but was closed down after Carte Blanche’s visit last year. Owner Susan van Niekerk re-started under the name Kairos. In December SADAG got a call from “Victor” who said that he was resigning in protest from Kairos because he was unskilled to look after mental patients.
“VICTOR”, FORMER KAIROS EMPLOYEE: They’re very aggressive and I don’t have training in how to treat them.
DEVI: How many hours a day were you working?
“VICTOR”, FORMER KAIROS EMPLOYEE: I can say 20 hours, because I never slept, because at night, the patients break things, they hit one another and then I have to stop them.
DEVI: Why are you telling us your story?
“VICTOR”, FORMER KAIROS EMPLOYEE: Because I feel very sad for the patients.
Van Niekerk rejected ex-workers’ gripes as sour grapes, but confirmed times are tough -- she has one resident nurse who has to look after 104 people and provide on the job training for 8 care workers.
DEVI: Is that enough?
SUSAN VAN NIEKERK, NGO OWNER: That’s not really enough. Our money does not cover more … they now charge R18 000 … but we have adequate care workers. There’s no money for training, there’s no money to get someone in from outside to come and train. All the care workers are living in, as part of their salary.
DEVI: As it stands now do you have money to operate?
SUSAN VAN NIEKERK, NGO OWNER: At this moment no, because the department didn’t pay me for two months.
DEVI: Again.
On Friday, the department confirmed that Kairos’ payments for February and March are being processed.
DEVI: Every single time I see you, you complain about the department, why are you putting yourself through this?
SUSAN VAN NIEKERK, NGO OWNER: Because I have to -- otherwise they’ll remove these people to where?
The hearings heard that the situation was the same at many NGOs, with unskilled and far too few workers.
BOITUMELO MANGENA, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: They had three boxes of medication and they were giving each person the same pill. So he asked them how are you giving these people the same medication when they all have different conditions. And the lady was just like listen I’m not a nurse, I’m not trained. I’m just following instructions. This is what I’m told to do.
But SADAG was shocked to hear at the hearings that the province DID in fact have money for better mental health services.
CASSEY CHAMBERS, OPERATIONS DIRECTOR, SADAG: Then to hear how that there was actually underspending on the budget every single year, was really alarming to us.
JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: The budgetary and financial crisis within the Department was mainly due to mismanagement, to incompetence and possible fraud.
DEVI LINK: If any good could come of this tragedy, it would be improved mental health services and care for psychiatric patients. But has the Esidimeni episode brought any real change?
Nomvula Nonjabe’s sister Khayakazi, a schizophrenic still traumatised by the move to an NGO, is now in Life Esidimeni’s Waverley Care Centre in Germiston.
NOMVULA NONJABE, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: When I took her December, she had quite a bad smell and I wasn’t sure why. So as I observed her at home, I realised that if you don’t tell her to bath, she won’t do it...so I realised there’s no supervision.
Nonjabe is on the family committee formed by Esidimeni families to engage authorities. They heard in testimony that agreements on patient care are in place...but they haven’t seen them.
NOMVULA NONJABE, FAMILY COMMITTEE: For me the journey continues and us keeping them honest, it’s a continuous work. It’s a lifetime commitment on my side.
Activist psychiatrist Dr Mvuyiso Talatala feels there’s much work ahead.
DR MVUYISO TALATALA, SPECIALIST PSYCHIATRIST: Life Esidimeni is the tip of the iceberg...there’s still a whole lot probably going on, especially in the rural provinces. I mean, if you look at education, the pit latrine story, I was actually shocked that the government has not dealt with the issue. And yet, we had an incident in 2014, and now it’s 2018, so I would not be surprised that in 2022, we have another Life Esidimeni incident.
Through their national helpline and this counseling container in Diepsloot, SADAG sees the gaps in the system daily.
CASSEY CHAMBERS, OPERATIONS DIRECTOR, SADAG: We’re very aware that the things like medication availability at community clinics or not having a psychologist or even a psychiatric nurse, never mind a psychiatrist at your community clinic, is a big problem. But also at district hospitals -- we don’t have enough beds. They’re completely overcrowded. There’s a new report coming out in the next couple of weeks on the “Stop the Stock-Outs” campaign and one of the most stocked out medication has got to do with mental illness. And I’m hoping that everyone that works in mental health takes Life Esidimeni and thinks about it every day.
ANDREW PETERSEN, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: You see, our excitement wasn't because we’re going to get the money, you know. Our excitement was that we have been vindicated. We told you this was wrong.
DR MVUYISO TALATALA, SPECIALIST PSYCHIATRIST: I just did a quick calculation -- they’re probably going to pay almost R2-billion and that is a lot of money out of the budget of health, but it’s punitive enough to send a lesson to our administrators that we should not listen to what our political masters say.
PROMOS
10 secs
VO: If any good could come of the Esidimeni tragedy, it would be improved mental health services and care for psychiatric patients. But has it brought any real change?

15 secs
VO: Have the families found what they fought for in the Esidimeni arbitration process?
BOITUMELO MANGENA, FAMILY MEMBER: You go into the arbitration process thinking I’m going to find answers. I’m going to find closure, I’m going to find healing. And the end comes and there’s none of that.

15 secs
VO: Judge Dikgang Moseneke’s award in the Esidimeni arbitration hearings was the moment families and their lawyers had been fighting for.
CHRISTINE NXUMALO, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: It was like the constitution suddenly, it was flexing its muscles.

The tragedy ensued after the Gauteng Health Department suddenly decided to move 1711 state patients from private Life Esidimeni facilities, where they had been housed for decades, to ill-equipped, unprepared non-governmental organisations. The department said it could no longer afford Life Esidimeni. At the NGOs, many of the severely mentally ill patients, in the care of the state, were left without medication, food, water and clothing to keep them warm through winter. 144 patients died. DEVI LINK TO CAMERA: Carte Blanche witnessed every step of the families’ journey to seek answers and accountability. It began when Christine Nxumalo discovered her sister Virginia Machpelah’s inexplicable death at a Pretoria NGO. STRAP: CARTE BLANCHE AUGUST 2017: Ethel, Ethel, Ethel, I want to see the room where she was in...want to see the condition of the place where she was staying… Moseneke awarded each family R1.2 million in damages for violated rights, trauma and funeral expenses. DEVI LINK TO CAMERA: All along, families have had two questions: Why, and who was responsible? The arbitration hearings were supposed to be a way to find truth, closure and redress. But after it all, emotions are mixed. ANDREW PETERSEN, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: It was never, never about the money. Andrew Petersen found his uncle Victor Truter emaciated at Mosego Home in Krugersdorp after the move. ANDREW PETERSEN, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: You know, the money helps, but it was always about sending a strong message to government...that also will create a momentum that will challenge this laidback sort of culture we have in government and civil service. Nxumalo and other families feel vindicated now that Moseneke joined all the dots. CHRISTINE NXUMALO, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: When I heard my sister’s name, it was like phew, this is real. It’s not some kind of a dream or some imaginary thing, you know, we experienced it. It was like the constitution suddenly, it was flexing its muscles…I swear it was almost a beautiful moment in such a sad situation. Over the years, Carte Blanche inspected the notorious NGOs -- they in turn pointed to the Health Department who had neglected to give them time, money and support. JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: These NGOs turned out to be sites of death and torture. Moseneke reserved his harshest words for the former top 3 at Gauteng Health: MEC Qedani Mahlangu, head of department Dr Barney Selebano and Mental Health Director Dr Makgabo Manamela. All three have resigned. The full record of the hearings will go to the police for investigation. JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Miss Mahlangu was responsible. She was the ultimate leader and commander of the project. The NPA said it’s received 140 dockets from police. It’s now up to them to decide whether anyone must be charged. // Boitumelo Mangena’s mother, Rahab, who suffered from dementia, was moved without their knowledge. Her brother found her at the overcrowded Takalani Home. BOITUMELO MANGENA, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: He said he found her sitting in the corner in a chair, no blankets, no shoes on, no socks on and she was still in her Life Esidimeni outfit. So in those two weeks that she had not … been changed or anything. While the siblings were trying to arrange to take her home, she died of a heart attack that they believe was caused by the conditions. BOITUMELO MANGENA, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: You go into the arbitration process thinking I’m going to find answers. I’m going to find closure, I’m going to find healing. And the end comes and there’s none of that. Survivors were mostly moved back to private facilities or state psychiatric hospitals. CHRISTINE NXUMALO, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: And one of the requests that we ask the Department of Health was that there must be an audit at the end of this process. We need to know exactly what happened to everybody. At provincial headquarters, Col Lungelo Dlamini said police have tracked down only 13 patients who went missing in the move. 1 had passed away. LUNGELO DLAMINI, GAUTENG SAPS SPOKESMAN: At this stage there are 49 people that are still missing -- the investigation is still continuing in that regard. The hearings revealed there are about 5000 psychiatric patients at NGOs in Gauteng. At the South African Depression and Anxiety Group, Cassey Chambers is concerned CASSEY CHAMBERS, OPERATIONS DIRECTOR, SADAG: A lot of these facilities were running before Esidimeni, so there are still patients that are at Takalani, Mosego Home that were kind of left behind and I think the real question is how we’re monitoring and checking up on those patients. Shammah House in Cullinan, outside Pretoria, had Esidimeni patients but was closed down after Carte Blanche’s visit last year. Owner Susan van Niekerk re-started under the name Kairos. In December SADAG got a call from “Victor” who said that he was resigning in protest from Kairos because he was unskilled to look after mental patients. “VICTOR”, FORMER KAIROS EMPLOYEE: They’re very aggressive and I don’t have training in how to treat them. DEVI: How many hours a day were you working? “VICTOR”, FORMER KAIROS EMPLOYEE: I can say 20 hours, because I never slept, because at night, the patients break things, they hit one another and then I have to stop them. DEVI: Why are you telling us your story? “VICTOR”, FORMER KAIROS EMPLOYEE: Because I feel very sad for the patients. Van Niekerk rejected ex-workers’ gripes as sour grapes, but confirmed times are tough -- she has one resident nurse who has to look after 104 people and provide on the job training for 8 care workers. DEVI: Is that enough? SUSAN VAN NIEKERK, NGO OWNER: That’s not really enough. Our money does not cover more … they now charge R18 000 … but we have adequate care workers. There’s no money for training, there’s no money to get someone in from outside to come and train. All the care workers are living in, as part of their salary. DEVI: As it stands now do you have money to operate? SUSAN VAN NIEKERK, NGO OWNER: At this moment no, because the department didn’t pay me for two months. DEVI: Again. On Friday, the department confirmed that Kairos’ payments for February and March are being processed. DEVI: Every single time I see you, you complain about the department, why are you putting yourself through this? SUSAN VAN NIEKERK, NGO OWNER: Because I have to -- otherwise they’ll remove these people to where? The hearings heard that the situation was the same at many NGOs, with unskilled and far too few workers. BOITUMELO MANGENA, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: They had three boxes of medication and they were giving each person the same pill. So he asked them how are you giving these people the same medication when they all have different conditions. And the lady was just like listen I’m not a nurse, I’m not trained. I’m just following instructions. This is what I’m told to do. But SADAG was shocked to hear at the hearings that the province DID in fact have money for better mental health services. CASSEY CHAMBERS, OPERATIONS DIRECTOR, SADAG: Then to hear how that there was actually underspending on the budget every single year, was really alarming to us. JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: The budgetary and financial crisis within the Department was mainly due to mismanagement, to incompetence and possible fraud. DEVI LINK: If any good could come of this tragedy, it would be improved mental health services and care for psychiatric patients. But has the Esidimeni episode brought any real change? Nomvula Nonjabe’s sister Khayakazi, a schizophrenic still traumatised by the move to an NGO, is now in Life Esidimeni’s Waverley Care Centre in Germiston. NOMVULA NONJABE, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: When I took her December, she had quite a bad smell and I wasn’t sure why. So as I observed her at home, I realised that if you don’t tell her to bath, she won’t do it...so I realised there’s no supervision. Nonjabe is on the family committee formed by Esidimeni families to engage authorities. They heard in testimony that agreements on patient care are in place...but they haven’t seen them. NOMVULA NONJABE, FAMILY COMMITTEE: For me the journey continues and us keeping them honest, it’s a continuous work. It’s a lifetime commitment on my side. Activist psychiatrist Dr Mvuyiso Talatala feels there’s much work ahead. DR MVUYISO TALATALA, SPECIALIST PSYCHIATRIST: Life Esidimeni is the tip of the iceberg...there’s still a whole lot probably going on, especially in the rural provinces. I mean, if you look at education, the pit latrine story, I was actually shocked that the government has not dealt with the issue. And yet, we had an incident in 2014, and now it’s 2018, so I would not be surprised that in 2022, we have another Life Esidimeni incident. Through their national helpline and this counseling container in Diepsloot, SADAG sees the gaps in the system daily. CASSEY CHAMBERS, OPERATIONS DIRECTOR, SADAG: We’re very aware that the things like medication availability at community clinics or not having a psychologist or even a psychiatric nurse, never mind a psychiatrist at your community clinic, is a big problem. But also at district hospitals -- we don’t have enough beds. They’re completely overcrowded. There’s a new report coming out in the next couple of weeks on the “Stop the Stock-Outs” campaign and one of the most stocked out medication has got to do with mental illness. And I’m hoping that everyone that works in mental health takes Life Esidimeni and thinks about it every day. ANDREW PETERSEN, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: You see, our excitement wasn't because we’re going to get the money, you know. Our excitement was that we have been vindicated. We told you this was wrong. DR MVUYISO TALATALA, SPECIALIST PSYCHIATRIST: I just did a quick calculation -- they’re probably going to pay almost R2-billion and that is a lot of money out of the budget of health, but it’s punitive enough to send a lesson to our administrators that we should not listen to what our political masters say. PROMOS 10 secs VO: If any good could come of the Esidimeni tragedy, it would be improved mental health services and care for psychiatric patients. But has it brought any real change? 15 secs VO: Have the families found what they fought for in the Esidimeni arbitration process? BOITUMELO MANGENA, FAMILY MEMBER: You go into the arbitration process thinking I’m going to find answers. I’m going to find closure, I’m going to find healing. And the end comes and there’s none of that. 15 secs VO: Judge Dikgang Moseneke’s award in the Esidimeni arbitration hearings was the moment families and their lawyers had been fighting for. CHRISTINE NXUMALO, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: It was like the constitution suddenly, it was flexing its muscles.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): With the arbitration award announced, we ask the Esidimeni tragedy brought any change? We investigate the current conditions of Esidimeni survivors and other psychiatric patients in Gauteng.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We unpack the arbitration award and reflect on the families' views of the outcome, while asking whether this experience has done anything to improve mental health care in Gauteng. After the Esidimeni tragedy, the surviving Gauteng state psychiatric patients were removed from the deadly NGOs and placed in state psychiatric hospitals or private facilities, some even into Life facilities. But are they better off now? There are complaints from family members that patients are still lacking proper care. The family committee says they want to have access to documents like the service level agreements between the provincial health department and the facilities - it is simply no longer good enough to hear that such documents exist. Meanwhile, other patients still remain at some of the NGOs where people died. Insiders tell us of the terrible conditions at two NGOs in Cullinan. Is the Gauteng Health Department just paying lip service when they promise to do betteR?
metadata.Summary: In the aftermath of the Esidimeni tragedy, the survivors of the Gauteng Mental Health Marathon project were moved to psychiatric hospitals and other facilities. In general, their living conditions are much improved from the NGOs where they were starving and freezing. But the family committee raises concerns that they do not have access to service level agreements between the health department and facilities to see whwther they are satisfied with the level of care agreed upon for their loved ones. Some families complain that patients are not getting proper care. Some facilities are not fit for purpose and there is still a lack of linen, toiletries and other things. One family member told us that her sister's ID was still with the owner of the NGO until very recently - the department had not taken steps to collect the IDs and Sassa cards until she queried it. We talk to family members and plan to visit facilities to see for ourselves. Even though the former Esidimeni patients were moved, some of the NGOs where patients died, remain open and other patients are still living there. Peter Mentoor, who used to work as a security guard at an NGO in Cullinan, says he left because he ccould not stand the way patients were mistreated. He says he was made to sleep in the ward with the patients and there were no qualified care workers at night. He says male and female patients are housed together and patients are not being fed and clothed properly. Meanwhile, the police and the Gauteng health department are also still looking for some patients who had gone missing during the move. The health department had simply lost track of nearly 50 patients -- for months, no one knew where they were. Some of these patients have since been found still living at some of the "death NGOs" We track what happened to these patients who have been found, and question what could have happened to those still missing.

metadata.Reason for legal: We must ensure that we are not violating any of the rights of vulnerable psychiatric patients. If the pre-arbitration agreement for the Esidimeni arbitration hearings, which determines how parties interact with the media, is still in place, we must not breach that.
